front: What quantity does each letter in the **SUVAT** equations represent?
back:
- ***s*** – displacement (m)
- ***u*** – initial velocity (m s<sup>-1</sup>)
- ***v*** – final velocity (m s<sup>-1</sup>)
- ***a*** – acceleration (m s<sup>-2</sup>)
- ***t*** – time interval (s)

front: Under what condition can the **SUVAT equations of motion** be used?
back: The SUVAT equations of motion can be used when the **acceleration is constant** (uniform) or **zero**.

front: State the four **SUVAT equations** of motion.
An object thrown vertically upwards slows down as it rises, so its acceleration is **..........** and its velocity at the highest point is **..........**
back: An object thrown vertically upwards slows down as it rises, so its acceleration is **negative** and its velocity at the highest point is **zero**

front:
**True or False?**

The **SUVAT equations** can be used for any object that is accelerating.
back:
**False.**

They can only be used when the acceleration is **constant**. They cannot be applied when the acceleration is **changing**.

front: In **SUVAT** calculations, why is the acceleration of a decelerating object given a **negative** value?
back: The SUVAT quantities are **vectors**. If the direction of motion is taken as positive, an acceleration that **opposes** the motion acts in the opposite (negative) direction.

front: On a **displacement–time graph**, what does the gradient (slope) represent?
back: The **velocity** of the object.

front: On a **velocity–time graph**, what do the gradient and the area under the line represent?
back:
- **Gradient** – acceleration
- **Area under the line** – displacement (distance travelled)

front: On an **acceleration–time graph**, what does the area under the line represent?
back: The **change in velocity**.

front: On a displacement–time graph, a horizontal line (zero gradient) shows that the object is at **..........**
back: On a displacement–time graph, a horizontal line (zero gradient) shows that the object is at **rest**

front:
**True or False?**

The area under a **displacement–time graph** represents the distance travelled.
back:
**False.**

The area under a displacement–time graph has **no physical meaning**. It is the **gradient** that gives the velocity.

front: What does a **curved line** on a velocity–time graph represent?
back: **Non-uniform (changing) acceleration**.

front: Define the **gradient (slope)** of a graph.
back: The **gradient** is the change in the *y*-value divided by the change in the *x*-value: $\text{gradient} = \frac{Δy}{Δx}$

front: What is the physical meaning of the **area under a graph**?
back: It represents the *y*-axis quantity **multiplied by** the *x*-axis quantity. For example, on a velocity–time graph, velocity × time = **displacement**.

front: How do you find the **area under a curved line**?
back:
- Divide the area into **rectangles** and **triangles**
- Calculate the area of each shape
- Count any remaining part-squares
- Add all the areas together

front: How do you determine the **units of a gradient**?
back: Divide the units of the *y*-axis by the units of the *x*-axis: $\text{units of gradient} = \frac{\text{units of}y}{\text{units of}x}$

front: To find the instantaneous acceleration at a point on a curved velocity–time graph, draw a **..........** to the curve and find its gradient
back: To find the instantaneous acceleration at a point on a curved velocity–time graph, draw a **tangent** to the curve and find its gradient

front:
**True or False?**

When calculating a gradient, you should use the two furthest-apart plotted data points.
back:
**False.**

You should choose two points that lie **on the line of best fit**, as far apart as possible. The plotted data points themselves may not lie exactly on the line.

front: Define a **scalar** quantity.
back: A **scalar** is a quantity that has **magnitude only**, with no direction.

front: Define a **vector** quantity.
back: A **vector** is a quantity that has **both magnitude and direction**.

front: What is the difference between **distance** and **displacement**?
back:
- **Distance** – the total length of the path travelled, regardless of direction (a scalar)
- **Displacement** – the straight-line distance and direction from the start point to the finish point (a vector)

front: How can an object have a **constant speed** but a **changing velocity**?
back: If the object is **changing direction**. Velocity is a **vector**, so a change in direction changes the velocity even when the speed (magnitude) stays the same.

front: **..........** is a measure of the displacement of an object per unit time, whereas speed is a measure of the distance travelled per unit time
back: **Velocity** is a measure of the displacement of an object per unit time, whereas speed is a measure of the distance travelled per unit time

front:
**True or False?**

**Mass** is a vector quantity.
back:
**False.**

Mass has **magnitude only**, so it is a **scalar**. It is **weight** (a force) that is the vector quantity.

front: Define the **components** of a vector.
back: The **components** of a vector are the **two perpendicular vectors** into which it can be split, which together have the same effect as the original vector.

front: For a force **F** acting at angle *θ* to the horizontal, state its horizontal and vertical components.
back:
- **Horizontal component:** $F_{x} = F \mathrm{cos} θ$
- **Vertical component:** $F_{y} = F \mathrm{sin} θ$

front: When a single vector is resolved, the two components produced are always **..........** to each other
back: When a single vector is resolved, the two components produced are always **perpendicular** to each other

front: State the two methods that can be used to **resolve a vector** into its components.
back:
- **Scale drawing** – an accurate diagram drawn with a ruler and protractor
- **Calculation** – using trigonometry (sine and cosine)

front:
**True or False?**

The two perpendicular components of a vector add together numerically to give the original vector's magnitude.
back:
**False.**

Because the components are **perpendicular**, they combine using **Pythagoras' theorem**, not by simple addition.

front: Define the **resultant** of two or more vectors.
back: The **resultant** is the single vector that has the **same effect** as two or more vectors combined. It is also called the **net** vector.

front: What are the two methods for adding vectors, and when is each used?
back:
- **Calculation** – used when the vectors are **perpendicular**
- **Scale drawing** – used when the vectors are **not perpendicular**

front: Describe how to add two vectors using the **triangle method**.
back: Link the two vectors **head-to-tail**. The **resultant** is drawn from the **tail of the first** vector to the **head of the second** vector.

front: When adding two **perpendicular** vectors by calculation, how are the magnitude and direction of the resultant found?
back:
- **Magnitude** – using **Pythagoras' theorem**
- **Direction** – using **trigonometry** (the angle from the horizontal or vertical)

front: In the parallelogram method, the vectors are drawn tail-to-tail and the resultant is the **..........** of the parallelogram
back: In the parallelogram method, the vectors are drawn tail-to-tail and the resultant is the **diagonal** of the parallelogram

front:
**True or False?**

The magnitude of the resultant is always found by adding the magnitudes of the individual vectors.
back:
**False.**

This is only true when the vectors act in the **same direction**. In general the resultant is found by **scale drawing**, or by **Pythagoras** if the vectors are perpendicular.

front: Define the **time of flight**, **maximum height** and **range** of a projectile.
back:
- **Time of flight** – how long the projectile is in the air
- **Maximum height** – the highest vertical point reached by the projectile
- **Range** – the horizontal distance travelled by the projectile

front: After release, what is the only force acting on a projectile (ignoring air resistance), and what is its effect?
back: The only force is **gravity** (its weight). This produces a **constant downward acceleration** acting on the **vertical** component of motion only.

front: At its maximum height, the **..........** component of a projectile's velocity is momentarily zero
back: At its maximum height, the **vertical** component of a projectile's velocity is momentarily zero

front:
**True or False?**

A projectile's horizontal velocity decreases as it travels through the air.
back:
**False.**

Ignoring air resistance, there is **no horizontal force**, so the horizontal velocity stays **constant** throughout the motion.

front: When solving a projectile problem, which quantity is common to both the horizontal and vertical calculations?
back: **Time**. The time of flight is shared by both components, so it links the horizontal and vertical parts of the motion.

front: Define a **free-body force diagram**.
back: A **free-body force diagram** shows all the forces acting on a **single object**, each drawn as a **labelled vector arrow**, with the object shown **free from contact** with any other object.

front: In a free-body diagram, what three things does each **force arrow** show?
back:
- **Magnitude** – shown by the length of the arrow
- **Direction** – shown by the way the arrow points
- **Type of force** – shown by a label or symbol

front: For a box sliding down a slope, name the **three forces** acting on it and their directions.
back:
- **Normal contact force (R)** – perpendicular to the slope
- **Friction (F)** – parallel to the slope, opposing the motion
- **Weight (W)** – vertically downward

front: When three forces acting on an object are balanced, their vector arrows form a **..........** triangle
back: When three forces acting on an object are balanced, their vector arrows form a **closed** triangle

front: What is meant by modelling an object as an **extended but rigid body**?
back: All parts of the object stay in the **same position relative to each other** when it moves — the object does **not** change shape or deform.

front:
**True or False?**

A free-body diagram should include the forces that the object exerts on other objects.
back:
**False.**

A free-body diagram shows **only the forces acting on that one object**, not the forces it exerts on anything else.

front: Define **Newton's first law of motion**.
back: A body remains **at rest** or moves with **constant velocity** unless acted on by a **resultant force**.

front: Define **terminal velocity**.
back: The maximum, constant velocity reached when the forces acting in the direction of motion are **balanced** by the forces opposing motion.

front: State Newton's second law of motion.
back: The **acceleration** of an object of constant mass is directly proportional to the **resultant force** acting on it: $Σ F = m a$

front: An object of mass 750 g accelerates at 11 m s<sup>-2</sup>. Calculate the resultant force acting on it.
Give two ways a car designer could reduce the forces opposing motion, to increase the car's terminal velocity.
back:
Any two from:

- Use tyres with **less grip**
- Make the car body more **streamlined**
- Reduce friction in the **engine** (better oil)
- Reduce friction in the **wheel bearings** (smoother surfaces/lubricants)

front: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity when the forces in the direction of motion are **..........** by the forces opposing motion.
back: A skydiver reaches terminal velocity when the forces in the direction of motion are **balanced** by the forces opposing motion.

front:
**True or False?**

If the resultant force on an object is zero, the object must be at rest.
back:
**False.**

A zero resultant force means the object is at rest **or** moving with **constant velocity** — this is Newton's **first law**.

front: Define **mass**.
back: The measure of the amount of **matter** in an object; the property that resists change in motion. SI unit: **kilogram (kg)**.

front: Define **gravitational field strength**.
back: The force per unit mass acting on an object in a gravitational field: $g = \frac{F}{m}$, measured in **N kg**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

front: State the equation linking weight, mass and gravitational field strength.
back: $W = m g$

front: What is the average gravitational field strength at the Earth's surface?
Why do all objects in freefall (with no drag) accelerate at the same rate, regardless of their mass?
back: Weight is proportional to mass ($W = m g$), so the acceleration $\frac{W}{m} = g$ is the **same for every mass**.

front: In **..........**, the only force acting on a falling object is its weight, so drag forces are ignored.
back: In **freefall**, the only force acting on a falling object is its weight, so drag forces are ignored.

front:
**True or False?**

A heavier object falls faster than a lighter object in freefall.
back:
**False.**

In **freefall**, all objects accelerate at the same rate, *g*, regardless of mass, since weight is proportional to mass.

front: In the electromagnet and timer method for determining *g*, what are the independent and dependent variables?
back:
**Independent variable:** height, *h*

**Dependent variable:** time, *t*

front: A graph of height, *h*, against *t*<sup>2</sup> is plotted for the electromagnet freefall experiment. What does the gradient represent?
back: Gradient = $\frac{1}{2} g$, since $h = \frac{1}{2} g t^{2}$ (as *u* = 0).

front: In the card and light gate method, a graph of *v*<sup>2</sup> is plotted against *2h*. What does the gradient equal?
back: The gradient equals ***g***, since $v^{2} = 2 g h$ (as *u* = 0).

front: Define the main systematic error in the electromagnet freefall experiment.
back: **Residual magnetism** remaining after the electromagnet is switched off, which causes the recorded time, *t*, to be **longer than it should be**.

front: In the ramp and trolley experiment, a graph of velocity, *v*, against time, *t*, is plotted. What do the gradient and y-intercept represent?
back:
**Gradient** = acceleration due to gravity

**Y-intercept** = initial velocity, *u*

front: In freefall experiments, each height, *h*, is repeated at least three to five times and an average value of *t* is calculated to reduce **..........** errors.
back: In freefall experiments, each height, *h*, is repeated at least three to five times and an average value of *t* is calculated to reduce **random** errors.

front:
**True or False?**

The cushion placed under the falling ball bearing is used to reduce random errors in the timing.
back:
**False.**

The cushion is a **safety** measure, to stop the ball bearing rolling away or damaging the surface — it does not affect the accuracy of the timing.

front: Define **Newton's third law of motion**.
back: Whenever two bodies interact, the forces they exert on each other are **equal in size**, act in **opposite directions**, and are of the **same type**.

front: State the two conditions needed for two forces to form a genuine Newton's third law pair.
back:
- The forces must be **equal in magnitude** and **opposite in direction**
- The forces must be the **same type**, acting on **two different objects**

front: A trolley (object A) exerts a force of 12 N on a wall (object B) during a collision. What force does the wall exert on the trolley, and why?
back: **12 N**, equal in magnitude, opposite in direction, and of the same type (contact force) — by Newton's third law.

front: A Newton's third law force pair consists of two forces of the **..........** type, acting on two different objects.
back: A Newton's third law force pair consists of two forces of the **same** type, acting on two different objects.

front:
**True or False?**

The forces in a Newton's third law pair always act on the same object.
back:
**False.**

Newton's third law force pairs always act on **two different objects** — forces on the same object are considered under Newton's **first law**.

front: Define **linear momentum**.
back: The product of an object's mass and velocity: $p = m v$. It is a **vector** quantity with SI unit **kg m s**<sup>**-1**</sup>.

front: State the equation for linear momentum, including the units of each quantity.
back:
$p = m v$

*p* in kg m s<sup>-1</sup>, *m* in kg, *v* in m s<sup>-1</sup>

front: A ball has a mass of 150 g and a velocity of 20 m s<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate its momentum.
A tennis ball (small mass, high speed) and a brick (large mass, low speed) have the same momentum. What does this tell you about the force each exerts on impact?
back: They would exert a **similar force** on impact, since their momentum — and therefore rate of change of momentum — is the same (for a given collision time).

front: Momentum is a **..........** quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction.
back: Momentum is a **vector** quantity, meaning it has both magnitude and direction.

front:
**True or False?**

An object moving to the left always has negative momentum.
back:
**False.**

The sign of momentum depends on which direction is chosen as **positive** — an object moving left only has negative momentum if **right** is defined as the positive direction.

front: Define the **principle of conservation of momentum**.
back: In a **closed system**, with no external forces, the total momentum before an event is equal to the total momentum after the event.

front: Trolley A (0.80 kg) travelling at 3.0 m s<sup>-1</sup> collides head-on with a stationary trolley B (twice the mass of A) and they stick together. Calculate their common velocity after the collision.
When trolley A exerts a force on trolley B during a collision, what force does trolley B exert on trolley A?
back: An **equal** force in the **opposite** direction, $F_{B-A} = - F_{A-B}$, by Newton's third law.

front: Two trolleys of unequal mass collide and exert equal and opposite forces on each other. Do they have equal accelerations? Explain.
back: **No.** Since $a = \frac{F}{m}$, the trolley with the **smaller mass** has the **greater acceleration**, even though the force on each is equal in magnitude.

front: In a closed system, momentum is conserved because colliding objects exert **..........** and opposite forces on each other.
back: In a closed system, momentum is conserved because colliding objects exert **equal** and opposite forces on each other.

front:
**True or False?**

If two objects moving towards each other have equal and opposite momenta, the total momentum of the system is zero.
back:
**True.**

Since momentum is a **vector** quantity, momenta in opposite directions cancel, giving a total system momentum of **zero**.

front: Define **moment**.
back: A **moment** is the turning effect of a force about a pivot.

front: Define **centre of gravity**.
back: The **centre of gravity** (or centre of mass) of an object is the point through which all of its weight can be considered to act.

front: What equation is used to calculate the moment of a force?
back:
$\text{Moment} = F \times d$

where *F* is the force in N and *d* is the perpendicular distance from the pivot in m.

front: Where is the centre of gravity located for a symmetrical object of uniform density?
back: At the object's **point of symmetry**.

front: What is the SI unit of a moment?
back: **Newton metres (N m)**, although newton centimetres (N cm) may also be used depending on the units given for the distance.

front: How does the width of an object's base and the height of its centre of gravity affect its stability?
back: A **wider base** and a **lower centre of gravity** make an object more stable, while a **narrower base** and a **higher centre of gravity** make it more likely to topple.

front:
A force is applied to an object at an angle to the pivot arm, rather than directly perpendicular to it.

Which distance should be used to calculate the moment of this force?
back: The **perpendicular** distance from the pivot to the line of action of the force, not the distance to the point where the force is applied.

front: For a system to be in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point must equal the sum of the **..........** moments about the same point.
back: For a system to be in equilibrium, the sum of clockwise moments about a point must equal the sum of the **anticlockwise** moments about the same point.

front: Why are door handles placed as far as possible from the hinge?
back: Placing the handle far from the hinge (the **pivot**) increases the **perpendicular distance** for a given force, producing a **greater moment** and making the door easier to open.

front: Under what condition will an object become unstable and topple over?
back: An object becomes unstable and topples when its **centre of gravity** is no longer positioned **above its base**.

front:
**True or False?**

A larger force will always produce a larger moment than a smaller force, regardless of distance from the pivot.
back:
**False.**

A moment depends on **both** the force and the **perpendicular distance** from the pivot — a smaller force applied at a greater distance can produce a larger moment than a larger force applied close to the pivot.

front:
In a balanced system, one force ($F_{2}$) produces a clockwise moment, while two other forces ($F_{1}$) and ($F_{3}$) each produce anticlockwise moments about the same pivot, where $d_{1}$, $d_{2}$ and $d_{3}$ are the perpendicular distances of $F_{1}$, $F_{2}$ and $F_{3}$ from the pivot.

How are these moments related when the system is in equilibrium?

**True or False?**

The centre of gravity of every object is located at its physical centre.
back:
**False.**

This is only true for **symmetrical objects of uniform density** — for irregular or non-uniform objects, the centre of gravity is not necessarily at the geometric centre.

front: Define **work**.
back: **Work** is the amount of energy transferred when an external force causes an object to move over a distance in the direction of the force.

front: State the equation for work done when a force acts parallel to an object's displacement.
back:
$Δ W = F Δ s$

where *F* is the force in the direction of motion (N) and *s* is the displacement (m).

front: A force acts at an angle *θ* to an object's displacement. How is the work done calculated?
back:
Only the **component** of the force parallel to the displacement is used.

If *θ* is measured from the horizontal: $W = F s \mathrm{cos} θ$

If *θ* is measured from the vertical: $W = F s \mathrm{sin} θ$

front: When a force acts at an angle to an object's motion, only the **..........** of the force parallel to the displacement does work.
back: When a force acts at an angle to an object's motion, only the **component** of the force parallel to the displacement does work.

front:
**True or False?**

A force that acts perpendicular to an object's displacement does work on it.
back:
**False.**

If the force has no component in the direction of motion (*θ* = 90°), cos *θ* = 0, so no work is done.

front: What happens to an object's energy when a force acts on it in the opposite direction to its motion?
back: The object **loses** energy, since work is done against the direction of motion.

front: Define **kinetic energy**.
back: **Kinetic energy** is the energy an object has due to its motion; it depends on the object's mass and speed.

front: State the equation for kinetic energy.
back:
$E_{k} = \frac{1}{2} m v^{2}$

where *m* is mass (kg) and *v* is speed (m s<sup>-1</sup>).

front: When a falling object loses gravitational potential energy, what happens to its kinetic energy?
back: It **gains** an equal amount of kinetic energy, since the lost gravitational potential energy is transferred into kinetic energy.

front: In the kinetic energy equation, only the **..........** is squared, not the mass or the one half.
back: In the kinetic energy equation, only the **speed** is squared, not the mass or the one half.

front:
**True or False?**

A 'loss of kinetic energy' should be given as a negative value.
back:
**False.**

Kinetic energy is a **scalar** quantity, so a loss in kinetic energy should not include a negative sign.

front: A body's speed increases from 12 m s<sup>-1</sup> to 45 m s<sup>-1</sup>. Does its kinetic energy increase by the same factor as its speed?
back: No. Since $E_{k} \propto v^{2}$, kinetic energy increases by the **square** of the factor the speed increases by.

front: Define **gravitational potential energy**.
back: **Gravitational potential energy** is the energy stored in a mass due to its position in a gravitational field.

front: State the equation for the change in gravitational potential energy in a uniform gravitational field.
back:
$Δ E_{p} = m g Δ h$

where *m* is mass (kg), *g* is the gravitational field strength (m s<sup>-2</sup>) and Δ*h* is the change in height (m).

front: What is the reference point (zero) for gravitational potential energy?
back: **Ground level** at the Earth's surface is taken to be zero gravitational potential energy.

front: Why does the equation $Δ E_{p} = m g Δ h$ only apply near the Earth's surface?
back: Because it assumes a **uniform** gravitational field, which is only a valid approximation close to the Earth's surface.

front: If a mass falls, it loses gravitational potential energy, which is converted **..........** other forms of energy.
back: If a mass falls, it loses gravitational potential energy, which is converted **to** other forms of energy.

front:
**True or False?**

For a falling object, the gravitational potential energy lost at the start equals the kinetic energy gained at the end (ignoring energy losses).
back:
**True.**

This follows from conservation of energy: gravitational potential energy is transferred into kinetic energy as the object falls.

front: Define the **principle of conservation of energy**.
back: The **principle of conservation of energy** states that energy cannot be created or destroyed, only transferred between forms; the total energy of a closed system remains constant.

front: Give two common physics examples of energy conservation between gravitational potential energy and kinetic energy.
back:
Any two from:

- A swinging **pendulum**
- An object in **free fall**
- **Skiing or skydiving**, where gravity causes motion and drag is negligible

front: When conservation of energy calculations are compared with real-life situations, what should be considered?
back: In reality there are always some **energy losses** from the system (e.g. to heat or drag), and these should be mentioned when comparing calculated, ideal values to real-life situations.

front: To apply conservation of energy, **..........** are usually ignored during the calculation stage.
back: To apply conservation of energy, **heat losses** are usually ignored during the calculation stage.

front:
**True or False?**

The principle of conservation of energy only applies to systems where no energy is transferred to the surroundings.
back:
**False.**

The principle applies to any **closed system**; energy can be transferred between forms (e.g. gravitational potential to kinetic), but the total amount remains constant.

front: A skier descends a slope, and 15% of the initial gravitational potential energy is not transferred to kinetic energy. How would you set up the energy equation to find the final speed?
back:
Equate 85% of the gravitational potential energy lost to the kinetic energy gained:

$\frac{1}{2} m v^{2} = 0 . 85 \times m g h$

front: Define **power**.
back: **Power** is the rate at which energy is transferred, or the rate of doing work (work done per unit time).

front: State the equation for power.
back:
$P = \frac{W}{t}$

where *W* is work done (J) and *t* is time (s).

front: What is the SI unit of power, and how is it related to joules and seconds?
back:
The **watt (W)**.

$1 \text{W} = 1 \text{J s}^{-1}$

front: Power is defined as the work done per unit **..........**.
back: Power is defined as the work done per unit **time**.

front:
**True or False?**

A lightbulb's power rating only relates to energy transferred by a force doing work.
back:
**False.**

Power simply means energy transferred per unit time, regardless of the type of energy; a lightbulb's power rating relates to **electrical** energy transferred, not mechanical work.

front: Which unit prefixes are commonly used with power in physics problems, and what do they represent?
Define **efficiency**.
back: **Efficiency** is the ratio of the useful power or energy transfer output from a system to its total power or energy transfer input.

front: State the equation for efficiency in terms of energy.
back: $\text{efficiency} = \frac{\text{useful energy output}}{\text{total energy input}}$

front: What units does efficiency have, and how can it be expressed?
back:
Efficiency has **no units**, as it is a ratio.

It can be expressed as a decimal between 0 and 1, or as a percentage between 0% and 100%.

front: In a lightbulb, electrical energy is converted to light and heat; the light energy is **..........** and the heat energy is wasted.
back: In a lightbulb, electrical energy is converted to light and heat; the light energy is **useful** and the heat energy is wasted.

front:
**True or False?**

What counts as 'useful' or 'wasted' energy is fixed and the same for every system.
back:
**False.**

Whether energy is useful or wasted depends on the system; for example, heat is useful in a heater but wasted in a lightbulb.

front: When solving an efficiency problem, why should you decide where the energy is lost from the system before starting the calculation?
back:
Because the given efficiency applies to a **specific stage** of the energy transfer.

Calculating first and deducting efficiency afterwards can lead to unnecessary work or an incorrect answer.

front: Define **density**.
back: **Density** is the **mass per unit volume** of an object.

front: State the equation for density and define each symbol.
back:
$ρ = \frac{m}{V}$

- *ρ* = density (kg m<sup>-3</sup>)
- *m* = mass (kg)
- *V* = volume (m<sup>3</sup>)

front: When converting a cubic unit, such as cm<sup>3</sup> to m<sup>3</sup>, why must the conversion factor be cubed rather than applied once?
back: Because **volume** is a cubic quantity, so all three dimensions must be converted, e.g. 1 cm<sup>3</sup> = 1 / (100)<sup>3</sup> m<sup>3</sup> = 1 × 10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup>.

front: When converting a smaller unit to a larger one, you **..........** the value by the conversion factor.
back: When converting a smaller unit to a larger one, you **divide** the value by the conversion factor.

front:
**True or False?**

A balloon is denser than a small bar of lead.
back:
**False.**

Density depends on **mass per unit volume**, not size. A balloon has a much **lower density** than lead despite occupying a larger volume.

front: What two quantities do you need to calculate the density of an object?
back: Its **mass** and its **volume**, with volume calculated using the equation appropriate to the object's shape.

front: Define **upthrust** (Archimedes' principle).
back: An object submerged in a fluid at rest experiences an upward buoyancy force (**upthrust**) equal to the **weight of the fluid displaced** by the object.

front: Under what condition does a submerged object float?
back: It floats when the magnitude of the **upthrust** equals the **weight** of the object.

front: Outline the two steps used to calculate the magnitude of upthrust on a submerged object.
back:
- Find the **volume** of the submerged object, which equals the volume of **displaced fluid**
- Find the **weight** of that displaced fluid using *m* = *ρV* and *W* = *mg*

front: The volume of the displaced fluid is equal to the **..........** of the submerged object.
back: The volume of the displaced fluid is equal to the **volume** of the submerged object.

front:
**True or False?**

An object always sinks to the bottom of a fluid unless it is less dense than the fluid.
back:
**False.**

An object sinks until the weight of the fluid it displaces equals its **own weight**. If this balance is reached before the object reaches the bottom, it **floats**.

front: Give the combined equation for calculating upthrust directly, and define the symbols.
back:
$U = ρ V g$

- *ρ* = density of the fluid (kg m<sup>-3</sup>)
- *V* = volume of displaced fluid (m<sup>3</sup>)
- *g* = gravitational field strength (N kg<sup>-1</sup>)

front: Define **viscous drag**.
back: **Viscous drag** is the frictional force between an object and a **fluid** which opposes the motion between the object and the fluid.

front: State Stokes' law and define each symbol.
back:
$F = 6 π η r v$

- *F* = viscous drag force (N)
- *η* = coefficient of viscosity (N s m<sup>-2</sup> or Pa s)
- *r* = radius of the object (m)
- *v* = velocity of the object (m s<sup>-1</sup>)

front: List the four conditions required for Stokes' law to apply.
back:
- The flow is **laminar**
- The object is **small**
- The object is **spherical**
- Motion between the object and fluid is at a **slow speed**

front: In **..........** flow, all the layers of a fluid move in the same direction and do not mix.
back: In **laminar** flow, all the layers of a fluid move in the same direction and do not mix.

front:
**True or False?**

Liquids become more viscous as temperature increases.
back:
**False.**

**Liquids** become **less** viscous as temperature increases, while **gases** become **more** viscous as temperature increases.

front: At terminal velocity, how do the forces on a sphere falling through a fluid balance?
back: The **weight** of the sphere equals the sum of the **upthrust** and the **viscous drag** force: *W* = *U* + *F**<sub>d</sub>*.

front: Define **terminal velocity** in the context of this experiment.
back: **Terminal velocity** is the constant velocity reached by the falling ball bearing when the forces acting on it are balanced (weight = upthrust + viscous drag).

front: State the independent and dependent variables in the investigation of viscosity using falling ball bearings.
back:
- Independent variable: **diameter of the ball bearing**, *d*
- Dependent variable: **terminal velocity**, *v*<sub>*term*</sub>

front: Why must the highest rubber band be positioned well below the surface of the liquid?
back: To ensure the ball bearing has already reached **terminal velocity** by the time it passes the first band.

front: The measuring cylinder must have a large diameter compared to the ball bearing to avoid the possibility of **..........** flow.
back: The measuring cylinder must have a large diameter compared to the ball bearing to avoid the possibility of **turbulent** flow.

front:
**True or False?**

Only one repeat is needed for each diameter of ball bearing tested.
back:
**False.**

The measurement should be repeated **at least three times** for balls of each diameter tested.

front: Why is a magnet used to remove the ball bearings from the measuring cylinder?
back: Steel ball bearings are **magnetic**, so a magnet held against the outside wall can retrieve them from the bottom of the tube without disturbing the liquid.

front: State the equation used to calculate the coefficient of viscosity, *η*, from this experiment.
back:
`\eta = \frac{2 r^{2} g \left(\rho_{s} - \rho_{f}\right)}{9 v_{term}}`

where *ρ**<sub>s</sub>* = density of the sphere and *ρ**<sub>f</sub>* = density of the fluid.

front: Define **Hooke's law**.
back: **Hooke's law** states that the **extension** of a material is **directly proportional** to the applied force (load), up to the **limit of proportionality**.

front: Define the **spring constant** *k*.
back: The **spring constant** is a property of a material that measures its **stiffness**; the larger the spring constant, the **stiffer** the material.

front: State the Hooke's law equation and define each term.
back:
$Δ F = k Δ x$

- *F* = applied force (N)
- *k* = spring constant (N m<sup>-1</sup>)
- Δ*x* = extension (m)

front: On a force-extension graph, what is the significance of the **limit of proportionality**?
back: It is the point **beyond which** Hooke's law no longer applies, i.e. the extension is no longer **proportional** to the applied force. It is identified where the line **starts to curve**.

front: What is the **elastic limit** of a material, and how does its position compare to the limit of proportionality?
back: The **elastic limit** is the maximum extension a material can undergo and still **return to its original length**. It always occurs **after** the limit of proportionality.

front: On a force-extension graph, the **..........** of the straight-line (Hooke's law) region is equal to the spring constant *k*.
back: On a force-extension graph, the **gradient** of the straight-line (Hooke's law) region is equal to the spring constant *k*.

front:
**True or False?**

On a graph of extension (y-axis) against force (x-axis), the spring constant is equal to the gradient.
back:
**False.**

When extension is plotted on the y-axis and force on the x-axis, the gradient gives Δ*x*/Δ*F*, so the spring constant is **1 ÷ gradient**, not the gradient itself.

front: Define **stress**.
back: **Stress** is the applied force per unit **cross-sectional area** of a material.

front: Define **strain**.
back: **Strain** is the **extension per unit original length**. It is a **dimensionless** quantity, as it is the ratio of two lengths.

front: Define the **Young modulus**.
back: The **Young modulus** is the ratio of **stress** to **strain** for a material undergoing elastic deformation; it measures how **stiff** a material is.

front: What are the units of stress, and why does strain have no units?
back: Stress is measured in **N m**<sup>**-2**</sup> (Pa), the same unit as pressure. Strain has **no units** because it is a ratio of two lengths (extension ÷ original length).

front: On a stress-strain graph, how is the Young modulus found?
back: The Young modulus is the **gradient** of the straight-line (linear) part of a stress-strain graph.

front: The **..........** tensile stress is the maximum force per original cross-sectional area a wire can support before it breaks.
back: The **ultimate** tensile stress is the maximum force per original cross-sectional area a wire can support before it breaks.

front:
**True or False?**

Strain is measured in pascals, the same unit as stress.
back:
**False.**

Stress is measured in **pascals** (N m<sup>-2</sup>), but strain is the ratio of extension to original length, so it is **dimensionless** and has no units.

front: Define the **yield point** on a force-extension graph.
back: The **yield point** is where the material continues to **stretch** even though no extra force is being applied to it.

front: What is the difference between **elastic deformation** and **plastic deformation**?
back:
- **Elastic deformation**: the material **returns to its original shape** when the load is removed
- **Plastic deformation**: the material does **not return** to its original shape when the load is removed, and occurs after the yield point

front: On a force-extension graph, how is compression represented, and how does this compare to how it is used in equations?
back: Compression is plotted on the graph as a **positive, increasing** value, even though it can be entered into equations as a **negative** value.

front: Why do force-extension and force-compression graphs for the same material differ from one another?
back: Because materials behave **differently** under tensile and compressive strain, so their force-extension and force-compression graphs are **not the same**.

front: The limit of proportionality is the point **..........** which Hooke's law is no longer true.
back: The limit of proportionality is the point **beyond** which Hooke's law is no longer true.

front:
**True or False?**

The elastic limit occurs before the limit of proportionality on a force-extension graph.
back:
**False.**

The **elastic limit** always occurs **after** the limit of proportionality.

front: Define **breaking stress**.
back: **Breaking stress** (or fracture stress) is the stress at the point where a material **breaks**.

front: What information can be determined from a stress-strain curve?
back:
- Up to what stress and strain a material obeys **Hooke's law**
- Whether it exhibits **elastic** and/or **plastic** behaviour
- Its **Young modulus**
- Its **breaking stress**

front: What physically happens to the atoms in a material at the yield point compared to at the breaking stress?
back: At the **yield point**, the atoms have started to **move relative to each other**. At the **breaking stress**, the atoms **separate completely**.

front: How is the Young modulus determined from a stress-strain graph?
back: The Young modulus is found from the **gradient** of the **straight part** of the stress-strain graph.

front: Breaking stress is not the same as **..........** tensile stress, which is also marked on many stress-strain graphs.
back: Breaking stress is not the same as **ultimate** tensile stress, which is also marked on many stress-strain graphs.

front:
**True or False?**

Breaking stress and ultimate tensile stress are always the same value.
back:
**False.**

**Breaking stress** is the stress at which the material actually fractures, which is **not the same** as the ultimate tensile stress marked on many graphs.

front: In Core Practical 3 (investigating the Young modulus of a wire), what are the independent and dependent variables?
back:
- Independent variable: the **load**
- Dependent variable: the **extension**

front: Why is a reference marker placed on the wire during this experiment?
back: To allow the **extension** of the wire to be measured **accurately** as the load is applied.

front: Give two precautions used in this experiment to reduce uncertainty in the final result.
back:
- Take diameter readings at **right angles** to each other, to check the wire is circular
- Take **six to ten readings** and find an average
- Remove the load and check the wire returns to its original length after each reading (a little **creep** is acceptable)
- Use a **Vernier scale** to measure extension

front: How is the Young modulus calculated once the gradient of the force-extension graph has been found?
back: Calculate the wire's **cross-sectional area** from its diameter, then find the Young modulus using the gradient of the force-extension graph and the original length and cross-sectional area of the wire.

front: Safety glasses should be worn during this experiment in case the **..........** snaps.
back: Safety glasses should be worn during this experiment in case the **wire** snaps.

front:
**True or False?**

A large amount of 'creep' after removing the load is acceptable, as it does not affect the results.
back:
**False.**

Only a **little** creep is acceptable; a **large** amount indicates the wire's **elastic limit** has been exceeded, which affects the validity of the results.

front: Define **elastic strain energy**.
back: **Elastic strain energy** is the **work done** in stretching a material, stored while the material obeys Hooke's law (before its elastic limit).

front: How is elastic strain energy found from a force-extension graph, and is this true for materials that don't obey Hooke's law?
back: Elastic strain energy is the **area under the force-extension graph**. This is true whether or not the material obeys **Hooke's law**.

front: Give the two equations used to calculate elastic strain energy for a material obeying Hooke's law.
back:
$Δ E_{el} = \frac{1}{2} F Δ x$

$Δ E_{el} = \frac{1}{2} k ( Δ x )^{2}$

front: For a non-linear (non-Hookean) region of a force-extension graph, how is the area under the graph calculated?
back: Split the graph into geometric shapes and sum their areas, then **count the remaining squares**, converting each square's value using the axis scales before adding it to the total.

front: For the linear region of a force-extension graph, the work done is the area of a **..........** triangle under the graph.
back: For the linear region of a force-extension graph, the work done is the area of a **right-angled** triangle under the graph.

front:
**True or False?**

The area under a force-extension graph only gives the work done if the material obeys Hooke's law.
back:
**False.**

The area under a force-extension graph gives the work done (elastic strain energy) whether or not the material obeys **Hooke's law**; only the shape of the area used to calculate it differs.

front: Define **wavelength** (*λ*).
back: The distance between a point on a wave and the same point on the next cycle of the wave, e.g. two crests or two troughs.

front: Define **amplitude** (*A*).
back: The magnitude of the maximum displacement reached by an oscillation in the wave.

front: Define **period** (*T*).
back: The time taken for one complete oscillation at one point on the wave.

front: What is meant by the **frequency** of a wave?
back: The number of complete wave cycles per second.

front: How are frequency *f* and period *T* related?
back: $f = \frac{1}{T}$

front: Wave speed *c* is the rate of **..........** of the wave.
back: Wave speed *c* is the rate of **movement** of the wave.

front:
**True or False?**

Frequency and period are directly proportional.
back:
**False.**

Frequency and period are **inversely** related, according to $f = \frac{1}{T}$ — as period increases, frequency decreases.

front: State the **wave equation** linking wave speed, frequency and wavelength.
back:
$v = f λ$

where *v* = wave speed (m s<sup>-1</sup>), *f* = frequency (Hz), *λ* = wavelength (m)

front: A wave has a frequency of 500 Hz and travels at 340 m s<sup>-1</sup>. What is its wavelength?
For a wave of constant speed, what happens to the **frequency** as the wavelength decreases?
back: The frequency **increases**.

front: Define **wave speed** (*v*), as used in the wave equation.
back: The speed at which a wave travels through a medium, measured in m s<sup>-1</sup>.

front: For a wave of constant speed, as the wavelength increases, the frequency **..........**.
back: For a wave of constant speed, as the wavelength increases, the frequency **decreases**.

front:
**True or False?**

For a wave of constant speed, wavelength and frequency are directly proportional.
back:
**False.**

They are **inversely** proportional — as one increases, the other decreases, since $v = f λ$ is fixed.

front: Define a **longitudinal wave**.
back: A wave in which the particles oscillate **parallel** to the direction of propagation and the direction of energy transfer.

front: Define a **compression**.
back: A region of **high pressure** in a longitudinal wave.

front: Define a **rarefaction**.
back: A region of **low pressure** in a longitudinal wave.

front: In a longitudinal wave, how do the particles oscillate relative to the direction of energy transfer?
back: **Parallel** to the direction of energy transfer.

front: Give three examples of longitudinal waves.
back:
- Sound waves
- Ultrasound waves
- P-waves caused by earthquakes

front: In a longitudinal wave, areas of low pressure are called **..........**.
back: In a longitudinal wave, areas of low pressure are called **rarefactions**.

front:
**True or False?**

Longitudinal waves can be polarised.
back:
**False.**

Only **transverse** waves can be polarised; longitudinal waves cannot.

front: Define a **transverse wave**.
back: A wave in which the particles oscillate **perpendicular** to the direction of propagation and the direction of energy transfer.

front: In a transverse wave, how do the particles oscillate relative to the direction of energy transfer?
back: **Perpendicular** to the direction of energy transfer.

front: Give three examples of transverse waves.
back:
- Electromagnetic waves, e.g. radio, visible light, UV
- Vibrations on a guitar string
- Waves on a rope or slinky

front: Can transverse waves be polarised?
back: Yes, transverse waves **can** be polarised.

front: A transverse wave shows areas of **..........** (peaks) and troughs.
back: A transverse wave shows areas of **crests** (peaks) and troughs.

front:
**True or False?**

Transverse waves show areas of compression and rarefaction.
back:
**False.**

Compressions and rarefactions are features of **longitudinal** waves; transverse waves show crests and troughs instead.

front: Define a **stationary wave**.
back: A wave formed when a wave is reflected with a 180<sup>o</sup> phase difference, creating a wave with a series of nodes and antinodes.

front: How is **wavelength** measured on a displacement-distance graph?
back: From one point on the wave to the same point on the next wave, e.g. two consecutive crests or troughs.

front: On a pressure-distance graph of a longitudinal wave, where is pressure highest and where is it lowest?
back: Highest at **compressions**, lowest at **rarefactions**.

front: On a displacement-distance graph of a longitudinal wave, where does maximum displacement occur?
back: **Halfway** between a compression and a rarefaction.

front: On a displacement-distance graph of a longitudinal wave, zero displacement occurs at compressions and **..........**.
back: On a displacement-distance graph of a longitudinal wave, zero displacement occurs at compressions and **rarefactions**.

front:
**True or False?**

A sinusoidal-shaped graph must represent a transverse wave.
back:
**False.**

Longitudinal waves can also look sinusoidal when plotted on a graph — check whether the wave travels parallel (longitudinal) or perpendicular (transverse) to the direction of travel.

front: What is the aim of Core Practical 4?
back: To measure the **speed of sound** in air between two points, using an oscilloscope and a signal generator.

front: What is the independent variable in Core Practical 4?
back: The **distance** between the microphone and the signal generator.

front: Give one control variable in Core Practical 4.
back:
Any one from:

- Same location for the experiment
- Same set of microphones for each trial
- Same frequency of sound for each set of readings

front: Which equation is used to calculate the speed of sound in Core Practical 4?
back: $v = f λ$

front: Why is frequency determined from the oscilloscope trace rather than read from the signal generator's dial?
back: To avoid relying on the accuracy of the signal generator's dial, which is a source of **systematic error**.

front: To reduce random error, the distance between the microphone and the signal generator should be made as large as **..........**.
back: To reduce random error, the distance between the microphone and the signal generator should be made as large as **is practical**.

front:
**True or False?**

Reaction time is a significant source of error in Core Practical 4.
back:
**False.**

The timing is done **automatically** by the oscilloscope, so reaction time is not a factor, making this experiment very accurate.

front: Define **interference**.
back: **Interference** occurs whenever two or more waves combine (by superposition) to produce a resultant wave with a new amplitude.

front: Define **path difference**.
back: **Path difference** is the difference in distance travelled by two waves from their sources to the point where they meet.

front: Define **stationary wave**.
back: A **stationary wave** (standing wave) is produced by the **superposition** of two waves of the same **frequency** and **amplitude** travelling in **opposite directions**, producing a wave pattern where the peaks and troughs do not move.

front: Define **coherent** (waves).
back: Waves are **coherent** if they have the same **frequency** and a **constant phase difference**.

front: Define **phase difference**.
back: **Phase difference** is the angle between the wave cycles of two points on a wave, or on different waves, that measures how far apart they are in their cycle.

front: What is the difference between a **node** and an **antinode**?
back:
- **Node**: a point of **no vibration**
- **Antinode**: a point where the vibrations are at their **maximum amplitude**

front: What is the difference between **constructive** and **destructive** interference?
back:
- **Constructive interference**: the resultant wave has a **larger** amplitude than any of the individual waves
- **Destructive interference**: the resultant wave has a **smaller** amplitude than the individual waves

front: What path difference gives **constructive** interference, and what path difference gives **destructive** interference?
back:
- **Constructive interference**: path difference = **n*λ***
- **Destructive interference**: path difference = **(n + ½)*λ***

where *n* is an integer (0, 1, 2, 3...)

front: How is a stationary wave usually produced in practice?
back: By a travelling wave and its **reflection** (e.g. off a fixed end, a reflecting plate, or the closed end of a tube) superposing.

front: What happens when two wavefronts travelling towards each other meet?
back: They combine by **superposition**, then pass through each other and emerge **unchanged** on the other side.

front: Two waves travel 6λ and 6.5λ respectively to reach point P. What type of interference occurs at P, and why?
back: **Destructive** interference. The path difference is 6.5λ – 6λ = λ/2, which is an odd number of half wavelengths, i.e. (n + ½)λ.

front: What is the phase relationship between points along a stationary wave that lie between two adjacent nodes?
back: All points between two adjacent nodes are **in phase** with each other.

front: What is meant by **monochromatic** light, and why does this matter for coherence?
back: **Monochromatic** light consists of light waves of a **single frequency**. Since coherent waves must have the same frequency, a coherent light source (e.g. a laser) must be monochromatic.

front: Path difference is generally expressed in multiples of **..........**.
back: Path difference is generally expressed in multiples of **wavelength**.

front: In a stationary wave, nodes are **..........**, while antinodes only move in the vertical direction.
back: In a stationary wave, nodes are **fixed**, while antinodes only move in the vertical direction.

front: A **..........** lamp produces incoherent light waves, whereas a laser produces coherent light.
back: A **filament** lamp produces incoherent light waves, whereas a laser produces coherent light.

front:
**True or False?**

Phase difference and path difference mean the same thing.
back:
**False.**

**Phase difference** compares how far apart two waves are in their cycle (peaks and troughs). **Path difference** compares how much further one wave has travelled along its path than the other. They are related but distinct concepts.

front:
**True or False?**

The nodes of a stationary wave move back and forth along the string as the wave oscillates.
back:
**False.**

Nodes are **fixed** points of no disturbance and do not move. Only the antinodes move, and only vertically (in amplitude), not along the string.

front:
**True or False?**

Two waves are coherent as long as they have a constant phase difference, regardless of their frequencies.
back:
**False.**

Coherent waves must have **both** the same **frequency** and a constant phase difference — matching phase difference alone is not enough.

front: State the equation for the **speed** of a wave travelling along a string with two fixed ends.
back:
$v = \sqrt{\frac{T}{μ}}$

where *T* = tension in the string (N) and *μ* = mass per unit length of the string (kg m<sup>-1</sup>)

front: Define **mass per unit length**, *μ*.
back: **Mass per unit length** is the mass of the string divided by the length of the string: *μ* = mass ÷ length, in kg m<sup>-1</sup>.

front: State the equation for the **fundamental frequency** (first harmonic), *f*<sub>0</sub>, of a stretched string of length *L*.
back:
$f_{0} = \frac{1}{2L} \sqrt{\frac{T}{μ}}$

where *L* = length of the string (m), *T* = tension (N), *μ* = mass per unit length (kg m<sup>-1</sup>)

front: At the fundamental frequency of a stretched string of length *L*, what is the wavelength of the stationary wave, and why?
back: *λ* = 2*L*, because at the fundamental (first harmonic) there is exactly half a wavelength between the two fixed ends of the string.

front: Increasing the **..........** in a stretched string increases the speed of the wave travelling along it, since *v* = √(*T*/*μ*).
back: Increasing the **tension** in a stretched string increases the speed of the wave travelling along it, since *v* = √(*T*/*μ*).

front:
**True or False?**

A thicker, heavier string (larger mass per unit length) under the same tension will vibrate at a higher fundamental frequency than a thinner string.
back:
**False.**

Since *f*<sub>0</sub> = (1/2*L*)√(*T*/*μ*), a **larger** *μ* gives a **lower** fundamental frequency, not a higher one — this is why bass strings on a guitar are thicker.

front: In Core Practical 5, what is the **independent variable** and what is the **dependent variable**?
back:
- **Independent variable**: either the length of the string, the tension in the string, or the mass per unit length
- **Dependent variable**: frequency of the first harmonic

front: How is the **first harmonic** identified when carrying out this experiment?
back: Increase the frequency of the vibration generator until **nodes** are seen at both ends of the string and a single **antinode** is observed in the middle.

front: How can the sharpness-of-resonance problem in judging the first harmonic be resolved?
back: Adjust the frequency while looking closely at a **node**, rather than the amplitude, since looking at amplitude is unreliable as the wave moves very fast.

front: If frequency, *f*, is plotted against 1/*L*, what quantity can be found from the graph and how?
back: The **wave speed**, *v*. The gradient of the graph is *v*/2, so *v* is found by doubling the gradient.

front: Name two safety precautions to take when carrying out Core Practical 5.
back:
Any two from:

- Use a **rubber string** instead of a metal wire, in case it snaps under tension
- If using a metal wire, **wear goggles**
- **Stand well away** from the hanging masses in case they fall
- Place a **crash mat** or soft surface under the masses to break their fall

front: The tension in the string is calculated using *T* = ***..........***, where *m* is the mass attached and *g* is the gravitational field strength.
back: The tension in the string is calculated using *T* = ***mg***, where *m* is the mass attached and *g* is the gravitational field strength.

front:
**True or False?**

To improve the resolution of results in this experiment, measurements should be taken over as small a range of lengths as possible.
back:
**False.**

Measurements should span a **suitable, large range** (e.g. 20 cm intervals over at least 1.0 m) to give greater resolution, not a small range.

front: Define **intensity** of a progressive wave.
back: **Intensity** is the **power** transmitted per unit **area**, where the area is perpendicular to the direction of the wave's velocity.

front: How is intensity related to amplitude and frequency?
back:
Intensity is proportional to **amplitude squared** and **frequency squared**:

$I \propto A^{2} f^{2}$

front: If the amplitude of a wave is doubled, by what factor does its intensity change?
back: The intensity increases by a factor of **4** (2<sup>2</sup>), since intensity is proportional to amplitude squared.

front: A point source emits a **spherical wave**. Explain, in terms of area, why the intensity of the wave decreases with distance from the source.
back: As the wave travels outward, its energy spreads over the **surface area of a sphere**, $4 π r^{2}$. Since this area increases with distance, the same power is spread over a **larger area**, so intensity decreases.

front: For a spherical wave, intensity *I* is proportional to , which is known as the inverse square law.
back: For a spherical wave, intensity *I* is proportional to **1/r**<sup>**2**</sup>, which is known as the inverse square law.

front:
**True or False?**

If a point source is moved to twice its original distance away, the intensity received halves.
back:
**False.**

Intensity follows an **inverse square law**, so doubling the distance reduces the intensity by a factor of **4**, not 2.

front: Define **refraction**.
back: **Refraction** is the change in **direction** and **speed** of light as it passes across a boundary between two different transparent media.

front: Define **refractive index**, *n*.
back:
The **refractive index** of a material measures how much light slows down when passing through it:

$n = \frac{c}{v}$

where *c* is the speed of light in a vacuum and *v* is the speed of light in the substance.

front: State Snell's law.
back:
$n_{1} \mathrm{sin} θ_{1} = n_{2} \mathrm{sin} θ_{2}$

where *n*<sub>1</sub> and *n*<sub>2</sub> are the refractive indices of the first and second material, and *θ*<sub>1</sub> and *θ*<sub>2</sub> are the angles of incidence and refraction, both measured from the **normal**.

front: A light ray travelling through air enters a glass block. Describe what happens to its speed and direction.
back: The light ray **slows down**, since glass is **more optically dense** than air, and it bends **towards the normal**.

front: A ray of light travelling along the normal to a boundary changes **..........** but does not change direction.
back: A ray of light travelling along the normal to a boundary changes **speed** but does not change direction.

front:
**True or False?**

A calculated refractive index of 0.8 could be correct for a glass sample.
back:
**False.**

Since the speed of light in a substance is always **less** than in a vacuum, refractive index must always be **greater than 1**. A value below 1 signals a calculation error.

front: Define the **critical angle**, *C*.
back: The **critical angle** is the angle of incidence, in the **more dense** medium, at which the angle of refraction is exactly **90°**, so the refracted ray travels along the boundary.

front: Derive an expression for the critical angle, *C*, at a boundary between a medium of refractive index *n* and air.
back:
From Snell's law with *θ*<sub>1</sub> = *C*, *θ*<sub>2</sub> = 90°, *n*<sub>1</sub> = *n*, *n*<sub>2</sub> = 1:

$n \mathrm{sin} C = \mathrm{sin} 90 ^{\circ}$

`C = \sin^{-1}\left(\dfrac{1}{n}\right)`

front: Can the critical angle be observed for light travelling from air into glass? Explain your answer.
back: **No.** The critical angle can only occur when light travels from a **more dense** to a **less dense** medium, and air-to-glass is the opposite direction.

front: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is exactly .
back: At the critical angle, the angle of refraction is exactly **90°**.

front:
**True or False?**

A material with a higher refractive index has a larger critical angle.
back:
**False.**

Since $C = \mathrm{sin}^{-1} ( 1 / n )$, a **higher** refractive index gives a **smaller** critical angle.

front: Define **total internal reflection** (TIR).
back: **Total internal reflection** occurs when the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, and the incident refractive index *n*<sub>1</sub> is greater than the refractive index of the material at the boundary *n*<sub>2</sub>, so **all** of the light is reflected back into the first medium.

front: State the two conditions needed for total internal reflection to occur.
back:
- The light must be travelling from a **more dense** medium into a **less dense** medium
- The **angle of incidence** must be **greater** than the **critical angle**

front: A ray of light in glass strikes a glass-air boundary at an angle of incidence smaller than the critical angle. Does total internal reflection occur? Explain.
back: **No.** Since the angle of incidence is less than the critical angle, the light **refracts** and partially transmits into the air, rather than being totally internally reflected.

front: Total internal reflection can only occur when light travels from a  medium into a less dense one.
back: Total internal reflection can only occur when light travels from a **more dense** medium into a less dense one.

front:
**True or False?**

"Internal reflection" is an acceptable way to name the phenomenon in an exam answer.
back:
**False.**

The full name, **Total Internal Reflection**, must be given — an incomplete name may not gain credit.

front: State the aim of the experiment to measure the refractive index of a perspex block.
back: To investigate the **refraction** of light through a **perspex block** by measuring the angle of refraction, *r*, for different angles of incidence, *i*.

front: In the refractive index experiment, why must the perspex block, light beam width and light frequency all be kept the same across repeats?
back: These are the **control variables** — keeping them constant ensures that only the angle of incidence affects the angle of refraction, so results can be compared fairly.

front: Describe how the entry and exit points of the light ray are marked on the paper during the refractive index experiment.
back: Small **'x' marks** are made at: a point on the incident ray near the ray box, where the ray enters the block, where the ray exits the block, and a point about 5 cm along the exit ray.

front: For a light ray exiting the perspex block, the angle of refraction is  than the angle of incidence.
back: For a light ray exiting the perspex block, the angle of refraction is **greater** than the angle of incidence.

front:
**True or False?**

When the angle of incidence at the perspex surface is 90° to the block, the ray refracts sharply.
back:
**False.**

At 90° to the surface (along the normal), the ray passes straight through **without changing direction**, so *i* = *r* = 0°.

front: State one safety precaution needed when using a ray box in this experiment.
back:
**Any one from:**

- Avoid looking directly at the light, as it may damage the eyes
- Stand behind the ray box during the experiment
- Keep liquids away from the electrical equipment, as the ray box gets hot

front: Define **plane polarisation**.
back: A wave is **plane polarised** when its particle oscillations occur in a **single plane** perpendicular to the direction of wave propagation.

front: Why can only transverse waves be polarised, not longitudinal waves?
back: **Transverse** waves oscillate in any plane perpendicular to the direction of travel, so they can be restricted to one plane. **Longitudinal** waves oscillate parallel to the direction of travel, so there is no perpendicular plane to restrict.

front: State three methods by which light can become polarised.
back:
- Polarising filters
- Reflection (from a non-metallic surface)
- Refraction

front: Explain why Polaroid sunglasses with vertically aligned lenses reduce glare from a wet road.
back: Light reflected from a horizontal surface is partially polarised in the plane **parallel** to the surface, i.e. **horizontally**. Vertically aligned Polaroid lenses block this horizontally polarised light, reducing glare.

front: Light reflected from a non-metallic surface is polarised in a plane  to the reflecting surface.
back: Light reflected from a non-metallic surface is polarised in a plane **parallel** to the reflecting surface.

front:
**True or False?**

Refracted light is polarised in a plane parallel to the transmitting surface.
back:
**False.**

Refracted light is polarised in a plane **perpendicular** to the transmitting surface, not parallel.

front: How can polarising filters be used to detect stress concentrations in a transparent material?
back: The sample is placed between two polarising filters at 90° to each other. Stressed regions **rotate** the plane of polarisation, allowing light through; **brighter** areas indicate **more** stress.

front: Define **diffraction**.
back: **Diffraction** is the **spreading out** of waves when they pass an obstruction, such as a narrow gap or the edge of an obstacle.

front: Define **Huygens' construction**.
back: A model in which every point on a wavefront is treated as a **point source of secondary wavelets**; the new wavefront is the tangent to these wavelets.

front: Which property of a wave changes when it is diffracted, and why?
back: Its **amplitude** decreases, because some **energy is dissipated** as the wave is diffracted through the gap.

front: When are the effects of diffraction most pronounced?
back: When the **gap or obstacle size** is approximately the **same as, or smaller than,** the wavelength of the wave.

front: X-rays passing through a crystalline solid are strongly diffracted, but radio waves passing between strands of human hair are not. Explain why.
back: **X-rays** have a wavelength (10<sup>-8</sup>–10<sup>-13</sup> m) close to the spacing between **atoms in the crystal**, so diffraction is significant. **Radio waves** have a much longer wavelength (0.1–10<sup>6</sup> m) than the gaps between hairs, so they are not diffracted.

front: Diffraction is the **..........** of waves when they pass an obstruction.
back: Diffraction is the **spreading out** of waves when they pass an obstruction.

front:
**True or False?**

Diffraction causes the wavelength of a wave to change.
back:
**False.**

Only the **amplitude** of a wave changes when it is diffracted; the wavelength remains **constant**.

front: Define a **diffraction grating**.
back: A plate containing a very large number of **parallel, identical, closely-spaced slits**, which produces a pattern of narrow bright fringes when monochromatic light is incident on it.

front: Define **angular separation** (of two maxima).
back: The difference between the angles of two orders of maxima, measured from the centre: *θ*<sub>2</sub> − *θ*<sub>1</sub>.

front: State the diffraction grating equation and define each term.
back:
$n λ = d \mathrm{sin} θ$

- *n* = order of the diffraction pattern
- *λ* = wavelength of light (m)
- *d* = slit separation (m)
- *θ* = angle between the normal and the maxima (°)

front: How is the slit separation, *d*, calculated from the number of lines per metre, *N*, on a grating?
back: $d = \frac{1}{N}$

front: How do you find the highest order of maxima visible for a given diffraction grating?
back: Set *θ* = 90° (so sin *θ* = 1) and calculate $n = \frac{d}{λ}$. Since *n* must be an integer, **round the result down**.

front: The maximum angle at which an order of maxima can be seen occurs when *θ* = **..........**°, giving sin *θ* = 1.
back: The maximum angle at which an order of maxima can be seen occurs when *θ* = **90**°, giving sin *θ* = 1.

front:
**True or False?**

If *n* = *d*/*λ* is calculated as 3.8, the highest order visible is *n* = 4.
back:
**False.**

*n* must be an integer and cannot exceed the calculated maximum, so a decimal result must be **rounded down** — the highest order visible is *n* = 3.

front: Define the **zero-order maximum**.
back: The **central beam** of the diffraction pattern, undiffracted, found at *θ* = 0°.

front: What is the aim of Core Practical 6?
back: To determine the **wavelength of light** using a **diffraction grating**.

front: State the independent and dependent variables in this experiment.
back:
- Independent variable: distance between maxima, *h*
- Dependent variable: angle between the normal and each order, *θ**<sub>n</sub>*

front: Why should the room be darkened and a set square used to align the laser and grating?
back: A **darkened room** makes the fringes clearer to see, and the **set square** ensures the beam meets the grating and screen at normal incidence, avoiding **parallax error** in measuring the fringe width.

front: Give two ways to reduce the percentage uncertainty in the measurement of *h*.
back:
Any two from:

- Use a grating with **more lines per mm** (gives a greater *h*)
- Use a **Vernier calliper** to measure *h*
- **Measure across all visible fringes** and divide by the number of fringes
- **Increase** the grating-to-screen distance, *D*

front: State two safety precautions for this experiment.
back:
Any two from:

- Use a **Class 2 laser** with a maximum output of 1 mW
- Never allow the laser beam to shine into anyone's eyes
- Remove **reflective surfaces** from the room

front: The accepted wavelength of a standard school red laser is **..........** nm.
back: The accepted wavelength of a standard school red laser is **635** nm.

front:
**True or False?**

Using a diffraction grating with fewer lines per mm reduces the percentage uncertainty in *h*.
back:
**False.**

A grating with **more** lines per mm gives a **greater** value of *h*, which **lowers** its percentage uncertainty.

front: Define **electron diffraction**.
back: The phenomenon in which electrons produce a **diffraction pattern** when directed through a thin film of graphite, providing the first clear evidence that **matter can behave as a wave**.

front: Why is a thin film of graphite used as the target in the electron diffraction tube?
back: Its **crystalline lattice structure** provides gaps between atomic planes similar in size to the electron's wavelength, so it acts like the **slits in a diffraction grating**.

front: What pattern is seen on the fluorescent screen, and what does it demonstrate?
back: A series of **concentric rings**, demonstrating that electrons show **wave-particle duality** by producing a diffraction pattern.

front: What effect does increasing the accelerating voltage have on the diffraction rings?
back: It **reduces the diameter** of the rings.

front: Why was the observation of electron diffraction significant?
back: It was the **first clear evidence** that matter, not just light, can behave as a **wave**.

front: If electrons behaved purely as particles, they would be distributed **..........** across the screen rather than forming a diffraction pattern.
back: If electrons behaved purely as particles, they would be distributed **uniformly** across the screen rather than forming a diffraction pattern.

front:
**True or False?**

Increasing the accelerating voltage increases the diameter of the diffraction rings.
back:
**False.**

Increasing the accelerating voltage **reduces** the ring diameter; a **lower** voltage increases it.

front: Define **matter waves**.
back: The wave behaviour predicted by de Broglie for small, fast-moving particles (such as electrons), where a particle's momentum is linked to an associated wavelength.

front: Define the **de Broglie wavelength**.
back: The wavelength associated with a moving particle, given by $λ = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{p}$

front: State the de Broglie equation and define each symbol.
back:
$λ = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{h}{p}$

- *λ* = de Broglie wavelength (m)
- *h* = Planck's constant (J s)
- *m* = mass (kg)
- *v* = velocity (m s<sup>-1</sup>)
- *p* = momentum (kg m s<sup>-1</sup>)

front: A person of mass 70 kg moves at 2 m s<sup>-1</sup>. Calculate their de Broglie wavelength.
back: $λ = \frac{h}{mv} = \frac{6.63\times10^{-34}}{70\times2} = 4 . 7 \times 10^{-36} \text{m}$

front: Why is the de Broglie wavelength of an everyday moving object, such as a walking person, never observed?
back: It is roughly **10**<sup>**20**</sup>** times smaller** than a nucleus, so it is negligible — the object behaves as a **particle**, not a wave.

front: The de Broglie equation shows that a particle's wavelength is inversely proportional to its **..........**.
back: The de Broglie equation shows that a particle's wavelength is inversely proportional to its **momentum**.

front:
**True or False?**

All moving objects, including people, exhibit observable wave-like behaviour.
back:
**False.**

Large objects have de Broglie wavelengths that are far too small to observe (around 10<sup>-36</sup> m for a person), so they behave as **particles**, not waves.

front: Define **transmission** (of a wave).
back: A wave **passes through** a substance and **emerges** from the other side.

front: Define **reflection** (of a wave).
back: A wave hits a boundary between two media and does **not** pass through, instead staying in the **original medium**.

front: State the law of reflection.
back: The **angle of incidence** = the **angle of reflection**.

front: What determines whether a wave is mostly transmitted or mostly reflected at a boundary between two media?
back:
- **Similar** densities → wave is mostly **transmitted**
- **Different** densities → wave is mostly **reflected**

front: Why are rough surfaces less reflective than flat surfaces?
back: A rough surface **scatters** the light in all directions, so a strong, single reflected wave is not produced.

front: A transmitted wave may have a lower **..........** than the incident wave, because of partial absorption as it passes through the material.
back: A transmitted wave may have a lower **amplitude** than the incident wave, because of partial absorption as it passes through the material.

front:
**True or False?**

Transmission is exactly the same process as refraction.
back:
**False.**

Transmission can **involve** refraction, but for transmission to occur the wave must pass through the material and **emerge** from the other side.

front: Define **transducer**.
back: A **transducer** produces and detects a beam of ultrasound waves, converting electrical energy into sound waves and vice versa.

front: Define **resolution** (in pulse-echo imaging).
back: **Resolution** is the amount of detail that can be captured by a pulse-echo technique; it depends on the wavelength used.

front: Why is gel applied to the skin before an ultrasound scan?
back: The **gel** matches the density of the boundary between the transducer and the skin, allowing the ultrasound signal to be easily **transmitted** rather than reflected.

front: In sonar, why is the total distance travelled by an ultrasound pulse equal to twice the depth of the water?
back: The pulse must travel **down** from the transducer to the sea floor, then travel the same distance back **up** again as the echo.

front: Pulse duration is a consideration because ultrasound transducers cannot **..........** and **..........** pulses at the same time.
back: Pulse duration is a consideration because ultrasound transducers cannot **transmit** and **receive** pulses at the same time.

front:
**True or False?**

Using a longer wavelength of ultrasound gives a better (smaller) resolution.
back:
**False.**

**Shorter** wavelengths give a smaller (better) resolution, since they diffract (spread out) less and more detail can be resolved.

front: Define **wave-particle duality**.
back: **Wave-particle duality** is the phenomenon in which light behaves as both a wave and a particle: it interacts with matter (such as electrons) as a particle, but propagates through space as a wave.

front: Define **photon**.
back: A **photon** is a discrete quantum (packet) of electromagnetic energy, proposed by Einstein to explain how light behaves as a particle.

front: What experimental evidence supports light behaving as a wave?
back: The **diffraction** and **interference** of light, as demonstrated in Young's double-slit experiment.

front: What experimental evidence supports light behaving as a particle?
back: The **photoelectric effect**.

front: Why does the wave theory of light fail to explain the existence of a threshold frequency in the photoelectric effect?
back: Wave theory suggests any frequency of light could cause photoelectric emission if the exposure time is long enough, since energy would build up gradually with each wave. This is not observed — only frequencies **above** the threshold frequency emit photoelectrons.

front: In the photoelectric effect, each electron can absorb only a **..........** photon.
back: In the photoelectric effect, each electron can absorb only a **single** photon.

front:
